en: Of course it is.
Max walks past the Zap-O-Matic. His hand finds the dial all by itself. Click.
Photo 1: everyone round the coffee table, the cake cut, Grandma with a fork, Grandpa with flour in his hair. Kalle and Flimmer wave from the Zap-O-Matic. Caption: "The cake was not a lie."
Photo 2: Zeldina measures the living-room wall with Mouldword's wand. Grandma holds the other end. Caption: "The attic would be available."
Photo 3: Archimedes in Grandpa's bathtub, Ramses between two slices of cake, undecided. Hermes comes through the door, too late. Caption: "Eureka. Again."
Photo 4: the goblins singing in the stairwell, signs with syllables in their hands, Grandpa conducting with the wooden spoon. Caption: "Cuddles-Pudding, hit the dough."
Photo 4: Grimtooth with a bunch of keys inspects Grandpa's oven. He complains to Model 08/15 or, without him, to Pixel. Caption: "Caretakers among themselves."
Photo 5: Max's empty spot on the sofa. Pixel lies on it, one eye open, looking at the door. Caption: "He's getting it."
That's a cliffhanger. I hate cliffhangers. I hate them almost as much as time travel.
He got the milk. Voluntarily. Without the password.
I need a moment. Or a tin. Ideally both.
Sorry, Max, but your milk is in another supermarket.
I stood so long under the bridge, counting rules and counting goats …
But today, my friends, today I chose: I'll sing! And nobody falls in the water!
An egg and some flour, a button, a light,
four worlds and a cake, but no milk in sight!
Clause fourteen b: what you borrow, you give back.
Clause one, brand new: you sing your own track!
And whoever's still sitting will stand up tomorrow …
… and geeeet iiiit!
Pressure normal. I'm letting go now. Farewell, door. It was an honour.
Caretaker, madam. Model 08/15. At your service.
That smells like …
Cake. That smells like cake.
Grandpa. What kind of machine is that.
The dragon egg.
The pharaoh's grain.
The Eternal Energy Cell.
And the Golden Remote is …
I've been to four worlds. I put a troll in a footbath, got a pharaoh to make a decision … talked an AI into madness and got a TV boss off his sofa.
For a shopping list.
And the remote? In the prologue you asked me if I'd seen it.
You said it out loud in World 4. Then came the anvil.
And Zappmann? The fairy lights blinked, you know him. Long story.
That's why the travel posters. That's why the box of remotes. That's why "preheat".
And what's the cake for? What was the whole end of the world for?
You were too lazy to go shopping.
You sent me into four worlds because you didn't want to go to the supermarket.
Long story, Grandma. Four seasons.
Grandma. These are … from an old lady who knows everything in advance. Happy birthday.
The machine sighs. The lamps go out one by one, the needle drops into the green, the bolt clacks back. Silence.
The wooden spoon falls out of the door and sticks to the floor. The door swings open.
A smell billows out of the machine. Warm, sweet, brown.
Nobody says anything. Zeldina looks at the ceiling as if checking for damp.
The hatch opens. Grandma stands in the opening, handbag on her arm, and sees: smoke, a cake, a princess, a cat, her husband.
Grandma takes a dog biscuit, bites into it, chews. Pixel makes his horrified face.
Konrad.
The train was on time. Miracles still happen.
So you're the new one.
The attic would be available.
And you are?
Finally someone who cleans.
Max. You're standing up straight. What happened?
Crunchy. Like Mother used to make.
Right. The cake comes downstairs. Everyone comes downstairs. Including the one with the wand and the one made of tin. It's my birthday, and I'm not celebrating it in an attic.
An … oven. A home-made one. With steam pressure and a mixer. Konrad model.
An egg. Free-range.
Flour. Type 405. Fine as dust. That was important, the dust thing.
A battery. AA. For the remote. It lasts forever if you don't use it.
Mine. The one I've been looking for for weeks. Yes.
For a cake. That's different.
I've been inside before. In the Zap-O-Matic. Once. To test it.
On Channel 999 it fell out of my pocket, right into Zappmann's studio. And I didn't want to admit where it was. Least of all in front of the cat.
1977. "Zappi's Dollhouse." I was the crafts uncle. Every Saturday.
In the last episode I demonstrated an oven live. It exploded. Live. With dough. All over Zappi.
Zappmann was never allowed in front of a camera again. And ever since, I only bake in secret. In the attic. With a safety lock.
The red circle. Today. Grandma's birthday.
I forgot it. Until last night. And shopping … the queue at the till, the parking, the people. I had a television that leads into worlds. So.
I was efficient.
If she notices, the world ends. Mine. That was never a lie. None of it was a lie. Just … grandly put.
Hildegard. You're early.
Say it.
Bakery. I said so. In World 2. Nobody listens to the cat.
I knew it. Since World 3.
The hologram. "Help me, Max." Who leaves an emergency message in a world he's never been to?
That counts as censorship.
That's why "brochures". My pile was right. My pile is always right.
He's telling the truth. It smells of cake and regret. Regret smells like wet dog, only more honest.
I'll never get over it. I said so. Now it counts double.
She didn't even raise her voice. That's power. Real power. I shall study her.
I'm only looking for a flat.
It's dark. Grandpa, it's got dark.
What's that?
That's a remote control.
I carried a remote control around for an entire world.
What are you saying?
Grandpa, Grandma is downstairs and we're locked up here with your work.
Okay. To be honest, that sounded like a final boss.
The glass of milk appears, the cow takes a breath, and the screen cracks. The Golden Remote in Max's hand blinks once. Cut to the attic.
Grandpa takes the egg out of the box and solemnly places it in the left socket. Then the flour sack in the right one. The machine swallows both with a clack.
Max hands it over. Glitter, a soft pop: in Grandpa's hand it is grey and worn.
Grandpa flips open the cover on the back, slides in the cell from the workbench, snaps it shut.
Grandpa points the detonator at the receiver and presses. The machine hums into life. Lamps blink, smoke rises, the needle on the pressure gauge creeps to the right.
The doorbell rings downstairs. Twice. A voice calls up from below.
The machine hisses. An iron bolt slides across the floor hatch, a red lamp blinks. The pressure gauge is in the red.
Konrad? It's me. I'm a bit early. The train was on time, imagine that.
Of course it's dark! It's evening! Four worlds in one afternoon, no day can take that!
The work. I built it while you were away. Twenty minutes of TV time is three hours at the workbench.
The remote! The golden one! You've got it! Give it here. No. Wait. The others first.
One: the dragon egg, unbroken model. Two: the pharaoh's grain, fine-as-dust model.
Three: the Eternal Energy Cell. Four: the Golden Remote. Now.
The detonator. Fully loaded.
Detonator. With buttons.
It's working! It's working! Twelve minutes, and everything will be different!
No. No, no, no. Not now. Not her. Not before it's time!
Dou… pressure overload! Safety lock! The work is protecting itself!
No one stops my dark work! She mustn't find out before it's complete!
No ad break. No cow. I'm missing something. I didn't know I could miss that.
Egg. Flour. Battery. Remote.
I said it out loud in World 4. Then an anvil came.
I'm saying it again now. Quietly. Without the anvil.
Nothing. Watch. This is your moment, not mine.
Your grandpa's shouting, the hatch is blinking, and you're just standing there. One of the three of you should do something.
The hatch. Look at it. Touch it. Then we'll know what we know.
Use the hatch. It won't open. But you only think about alternatives once you've tried. That's how you are.
There's a princess standing around with a Dark Lord's wand. That's not a coincidence. That's casting.
Zeldina told you what she uses the wand for. Doors. Landlords. There's a door here.
Talk to Zeldina and ask her about the hatch. She'll prise the bolt open. I'd have done it myself, but I have no thumbs.
Something is growing behind the little window. When the thing stops, the something will want out. Someone has to hold the door.
There's a robot here who's been holding doors since he was built. Ask him. Politely. He's Austrian.
No robot here. But in the compulsory pocket there's something that jams and sticks and has never once complained.
Talk to Model 08/15 and let him hold the oven door. He'll say hello to it. Let him.
Jam the wooden spoon in the oven door. It survived a Dark Lord, it'll survive dough.
The machine only listens to what your grandpa had in his hand. Had. Past tense. Where is it now?
Everything people drop ends up under armchairs. Look under the armchair. Then switch to me, I fit under there.
The remote is under the armchair, the cell right at the back. You take the remote, I fetch the cell, you put it in.
I hate it when I have to list work steps.
You've got a remote. There's a receiver over there. For four worlds you've done nothing but point and press.
Your grandpa shouts especially loudly at one button. People always shout at the right one.
Point the detonator at the receiver and press the red button. Stop. Secure the oven door first, or you'll be eating dough. Again.
I'm still thinking. It looks like staring. It is staring. But with substance.
All done. The hatch is about to open. I'd sit down now if I were you. I'm not you. I'm already sitting.
The dragon egg. Warm, heavy, with a scale pattern. Grandpa says it has to stay in one piece. I'm carrying it like a raw egg. Which it is.
An egg. Just an egg. I saved a world for it. It's looking at me like that's normal.
Size M, free-range, dragon. It doesn't say that on it. But it should.
The golden sack of pharaoh's grain. With a seal. It rustles elegantly when I move it.
A whole pharaoh couldn't make up his mind, but he was sure about the grain. I respect this sack.
A sack of flour. The gold was just the packaging. Grandpa calls it marketing.
The Eternal Energy Cell. It hums very quietly. When I hold it to my ear, I can hear the future. It sounds like rain.
It glows in the dark of my bag. My bag has mood lighting now.
A battery. A very good battery. I switched off an AI for it. The remote will be happy.
It says "eternal" on the side. I believe it. This battery will outlive us all. And the remote too.
The Golden Remote, without the cell. Grey and light. Like a trophy that remembers it's made of plastic.
The battery compartment at the back is open. Empty. Waiting. Like me on a Friday waiting for the end of school.
An egg. Three minutes, soft, with salt. I'm not saying that as a threat. I'm saying it as a vision.
Flour. You make things with a crust out of it. I told you in Egypt. I'm not saying it again. Oh, I just did.
I've been holding doors since 2077. This one is warm. I'll hold it anyway. Greetings, door.
The hatch is properly locked. I don't open anything that's proper. Greetings.
Zeldina, the hatch. Can you get it open?
The pressure. The needle. As long as that thing is running, the hatch stays shut.
Nothing. He's got nothing in his hand. He's waving empty hands around.
Zeldina, Grandpa, the robot and me. If we get the hatch open now, Grandma comes in and the thing is still running.
Can you hold the oven door?
The wooden spoon. In the oven door. It jams. It sticks. It holds. I call that a bond.
The tin head has it under control. The spoon stays where it is.
Something's blinking under the armchair. Red. In rhythm. Like a notification.
Still blinking. Unread message under the armchair. Grandpa has notifications turned off.
There. The remo… the detonator. The cover's open. The cell is gone.
Something's glowing back there. Right at the back against the wall. My arm is too short and the chair is too heavy.
Give it here. No, don't lick it. Give it here.
Cell in, cover shut. Detonator. With buttons. I sound like Grandpa.
An ordinary remote. Volume up, volume down, channel, mute and a red button at the top. The red one is the same on all of them.
The red button is worn. Like on every remote in the world. Everyone presses red first.
The red button means stop. On every remote in the world.
Chocolate. That's chocolate. Why is the end of the world made of chocolate.
The wand opens doors, not machines. And Zeldina hasn't let go of it anyway.
The spoon doesn't fit in the bolt. It just sticks to it.
No cell, no power. I know that from my phone.
Give Grandpa the detonator? He's dropped it once already. And he's used it once already.
Zeldina rams the black wand into the bolt and twists. Sparks. The bolt springs open. The hatch still doesn't budge.
Max points the detonator at the receiver. Four buttons light up. The player chooses.
The machine gets louder. Much louder. The needle trembles.
The machine changes channel. In the oven-door window, the dough is a newsreader for a moment, then dough again.
Grandpa keeps talking, but you can't hear a thing. The machine hums on undisturbed.
Max presses stop. The oven door flies open, and a gush of brown dough splats into Max's face. The door slams shut, the machine hums on, the needle creeps back into the red.
The detonator! Where's the detonator? I had it! I had it when the doorbell rang!
You've got it! Give it to me! No! Don't point it at the work!
Not the red button!
Not louder! It can already hear!
You see! You see what happens when you don't respect my work!
The cell is nothing without the capsule! Nothing! A button with nothing to push it!
Yes! Give it … no. No, I don't even want it. My hands are shaking. You do it.
Then the thing has to stop running. And who tells the thing to stop?
The one with the detonator. Look at your grandpa. What's in his hand?
He's holding an oven door and saying hello to it. That's the politest robot I know. I know two.
A wooden spoon is holding back the end of the world. Mouldword would have cried.
I'm not crying. I'm just close.
I fit under there. I don't like saying I fit anywhere.
Switch to me. And don't look.
Dust. A sock. A biscuit from 1998. And a glowing cell. I'll take the cell. I'm making a note of the biscuit.
Milk prices are rising, he said. Grandfathers continue to forget birthdays. That was very short. And very clear.
Keep that button. We'll need it later. For every lecture.
Hold the door first, then stop it. In that order. Like with tins: open first, then eat.
And don't lick that off. Actually, do. Lick it off. Report back.
The tin of tuna doesn't hold oven doors. It holds me. That's its job.
A bolt. Iron. Thick. Cute.
Bolt's open. But something's pushing against it from inside. Something big. Something soft.
Then stop it. And hold the oven door first. I once saw what a dragon does when you open the door too early.
I prise open bolts, not ovens. There are specialists for that.
The hatch. An iron bolt as thick as my arm, and a red lamp that's laughing at me.
I pulled on the bolt. The bolt pulled back. It won. I've got a mark on my hand.
Locked. Properly locked. That's not a bug, that's a feature.
Grandpa's work. Copper pipes, rivets, a pressure gauge in the red and a small round window. Looks like a boss from a steampunk game.
If this thing has a second phase, I'm running. Final bosses always have a second phase.
Behind the window something brown is swelling. It's growing. I don't know if it can see me.
The needle is in the red. Red is never good. Except on trainers.
I tap the glass. The needle trembles. I stop tapping. We understand each other.
Two sockets, both closed. The egg and the flour are in there. They're legendary artefacts. That's what they are. Definitely.
A legendary egg. Legendary flour. In my head someone with a deep voice says: "It's dangerous to go alone."
A small dish antenna. That's where Grandpa pointed the detonator. The remote. The thing.
The antenna turns a little when I move. It likes me. Or it wants something from me.
Grandpa. Red face, white hair, screwdriver behind his ear. If that's the final boss, the rest was the tutorial.
He's sweating. He's smiling. He's sweating while smiling. Grandpa has nothing to hide, except everything.
Hands off, he says. I'm not touching it. I'm scared it'll touch back.
The moon. From outside this probably looks cosy.
A star is blinking. Probably a satellite. It's bound to be watching Channel 999 and laughing.
Too small for me, too high for Pixel, too far for Grandma. No way out.
The Zap-O-Matic. Still running. Channel 999 shows an empty studio and a golden sofa. No thanks.
The sofa on Channel 999 is slowly turning towards me. I turn away. It's learned.
Time's running, Grandma's coming, the hatch is shut. This is an episode without a pause button.
Grandpa's lost-and-found box. On top is a bag of dog biscuits. The ones from the future.
The biscuits from the old lady who knows everything in advance. Maybe she knows what they're for, too.
Grandpa's lost-and-found box. He really doesn't throw anything away. Neither do I any more, it seems.
On top is a voucher for "One lawn mowing". From me. From Year 2. He kept it.
Konrad? Why does it smell of burnt sugar in here?
I'm coming up now. I'm not counting to three. I'm just coming.
The world will become soft! Soft and warm!
Twelve more minutes, and everyone in this house will know my name!
No one leaves this attic until it has risen!
Hands off! That's set to the exact degree! The exact degree!
I always thought he was harmless. For fourteen years.
Fourteen years. I slept on his lap.
"Soft and warm." That's either the end of the world or something you can lie on.
I don't know which I'm hoping for.
I'd fit under it. Not through iron, sadly. I've never tried. I'm not trying.
Something brown that grows and smells warm. I'm hungry and scared. My two favourite feelings.
It smells. It doesn't smell like the end of the world.
The end of the world smells of sulphur, every tomcat knows that. This smells of … I'm not saying it.
The television is the only way out. And the only way in.
Think about what tends to come in through ways in.
The dog biscuits survived the journey. Sadly. Some things are more eternal than energy cells.
You're taking the dog biscuits. Now. While your grandma is coming up the stairs.
I didn't see anything.
Eureka! No, wait, wrong occasion. A locked attic? A lever! You need a lever!
Max! Kssh! I can't get out, I'm static! But I'm keeping my fingers crossed! I don't have fingers! Kssh!
Locked in? Then you need the Gerd Glück skeleton key, for a limited time only, now with free Gerd!
Greetings, lad. Locked, you say? Properly? Then I'm coming. Order is my speciality.
I'll be back. I said so. I keep my word. I keep hold of anything you hand me.
Supple, lad. Olive oil, cold-pressed. I feel brand new. What shall I hold?
Your ally is in another channel!
Max! Dude! The caretaker is on his way to Konner number 31. I can send you meow-Morse. Does that help?
Thought so. Good luck, man. You've still got the spoon!
A call for help via television. Like a group chat, only with a dial.
Channel 3. Zeldina! We're stuck, Grandpa's lost it and the door's locked!
Emergency. Not a viewing.
Channel 7. Archimedes! Ramses! Anyone!
Thanks. Very helpful. All of you.
Channel 42. Hello? Anyone with joints?
No.
Channel 999. Flimmer? Anyone?
Zappmann?
Good. Good for him.
Zeldina, what was that magic wand?
Was the tower worth it?
How are the joints?
For landlords?
And what are you looking for now?
Zeldina climbs out of the screen, dusts herself off and looks around as if she's at a viewing.
Model 08/15 steps out of the screen, bows with a clank and looks at the machine like a stain that has to go.
Nobody is sitting on the golden sofa. There's a note on it: "Got up. Z."
We need help. From over there. You know people there. I know food there.
Nowhere yet. That's the worrying part.
If you'd oiled the tin head, he'd be here now.
I'm not saying that as a reproach. I'm saying it for the record.
Shall I help? Or not? I'm thinking about it. I'll get back to you. Maybe.
Thank you, Max! But the princess is … oh no, there she is.
A locked door, a landlord who's lost it and an attic? I'm coming. That's my core competence.
Sloping ceiling, skylight, period building. What about the service charges?
Everything's a viewing if you look long enough. Where's the fire?
So. A princess, a cat, a boy and an inventor who's lost it. That's enough. That's been enough in every fairy tale.
So. A princess, a cat, a boy, a caretaker and an inventor who's lost it. That's practically a flatshare.
Mouldword's. He left it behind when he went back to school. I use it for doors that stick. And for landlords.
Seven floors, no lift, a dragon as a lodger. I love it. I'm still looking. You always keep looking.
They stick too. Usually on the deposit.
Something with a lift. And without a dragon. He can come to visit, though, he always brings coal.
A sign. A very clear sign.
"Today only." I knew it was coming. It's been written in the stars for four worlds. And on the display stand.
The last quest. No dragons at all.
The milk is right at the back. Of course. Every shop is a dungeon, and the milk is the treasure in the last room.
No static. No channel. Just a door that opens by itself. I've never done this before either.
Cut. Supermarket entrance, late in the evening. Max stands in front of the glass door, hands not in his pockets.
The door slides open. Max goes inside. The light from the shop falls onto the pavement. Fade to black.
I'll be back. With the tea towel.
The cake. Lopsided, brown, warm. That's the final boss. I've cut into it.
The cake is still steaming. It's been through four worlds, a dragon and a final battle. It looks very relaxed for that.
A garland. Grandpa put it up while I was in antiquity. With drawing pins. In Grandma's wallpaper.
The garland is crooked. Grandpa says it's on purpose. Grandma says it's Grandpa. They're both right.
Small presents. One is a remote-control cover. Grandpa is learning. Slowly.
One present is wrapped in newspaper. In the TV guide. I recognise the dog-ears.
In every photo Grandma looks like someone forgot her birthday. Now I know why.
In the newest photo Grandma is smiling. It hasn't been taken yet. But I already know what it looks like.
The sofa. My home. It looks smaller. Or I'm bigger. Both unlikely.
The Zap-O-Matic is in the living room now. Grandpa says TV on birthdays is a tradition. Grandma says nothing. That's worse.
The Zap-O-Matic is showing a test card. Flimmer is waving in the corner. I wave back. Nobody here understands why.
This is where the remote used to be. Now it's here again. It fits the dust outline exactly.
I put the remote exactly into the dust outline. Fits. The sofa sighs. So do I.
The caretaker is washing up. Without being asked. Grandma is watching him like a sunset.
He dries every cup separately and says "Greetings" to each one. Grandma gave him an apron. He's weeping oil.
Page 3. An egg, soft-boiled. Something made of flour. Batteries. Milk.
Pixel. Your shopping list is Grandpa's shopping list.
At the very bottom of page three it also says: "Next year: sofa for two." In Pixel's paw-writing.
Grandma, did you know Grandpa used to be on television?
Grandpa, the password.
I'll get it.
Later. Milk first. You finish one quest before you start the next.
No. This is a one-person quest. Stay. Grandma still has questions about the rent.
I'm off, then. To the supermarket. Voluntarily. Nobody say anything.
Good evening. Happy birthday, Mum.
I'm not asking. I had the late shift. I'll ask tomorrow.
Konrad, this is your shopping list. You didn't buy any of it, did you?
Eggs. Flour. Batteries. Find the remote.
And milk. Where's the milk?
The cake is on the coffee table. It's lopsided, steaming and looks magnificent. Grandma cuts the first slice.
The door opens. Max's mother comes in, jacket still on, keys in hand. She sees a robot washing up, a princess with cake, a cat on the cupboard. She takes one deep breath.
She picks a crumpled note up off the coffee table, right next to the remote.
Silence. Pixel lets himself drop from the cupboard towards the sofa. Grandpa pulls a second note out of his cardigan and holds it out to Max. It has something with lots of characters on it.
Max looks at the note. Then he stands up. He doesn't take it.
Pixel misses the sofa and falls off the cupboard onto the carpet in shock.
It's risen. I'll give you that, Konrad. It's risen.
A cake without milk? Konrad.
That's where I met him. I was in the front row when the oven exploded. The dough hit me. I thought: he's the one.
The boy is all right. You're not, Konrad. But the boy is.
He apologised. With a cake. He's baked me one every year since. Usually none of them explode.
Seventy minutes at steam pressure, mixer on setting …
Milk was … milk wasn't on any channel.
In a minute. I wrote it down. It's somewhere I look every day.
The password. A scientist's word of honour. Here.
Max. The password. You didn't take it.
Milk was on every channel. For five seconds. Three times. I was the only one watching.
The sofa. My territory. I lent it to you humans for a few worlds. The loan period has expired.
Zeldina is checking the wallpaper for mould. She's asking Grandma about the rent. Grandma is answering. I'm scared.
She asked Grandma whether the castle has been renovated. Grandma said yes. I think she meant the bathroom.
I was the only one with a plan the whole time. Salmon wasn't on it. I'll never forgive the universe for that.
He … He said … Did anyone record that? Grandpa! Was the camera running?
I'm saying something. I'm just saying it later. When I can sit again.
Romantic. With dough.
Shall I come with you? I know a thing or two about searching.
Kid, I've explained everything. Now I have to get back to tinkering. The future doesn't screw itself together.
Later, Max. I've just had an idea. It's half finished. Like all my ideas.
Hi, Grandpa. The password?
That's a TV.
Sounds like a season with too many episodes.
How about one piece of the password per thing?
No.
Pixel is lying on the power cable. He picked the warmest spot in the house. Respect.
He weighs as much as a moving box. A full one.
Grandpa's toolbox. Screwdriver, wire, tuna. The usual filing system.
Under the wire there's a note: "Tools for emergencies. And for Pixel." I think that's the same thing.
A tin of tuna. Emergency rations. Grandpa thinks of everything. Except Wi-Fi.
A can opener. The crank kind. Like an app, but with muscles.
I'm not in the mood to open it with my teeth.
Pssht.
He talks.
In brine.
A cat with a help function. Like a chatbot, only hairier.
The Zap-O-Matic. Off. As long as Pixel's on the cable, Grandpa won't switch it on.
The screen is black. I can see my reflection. It looks just as bored as I am.
It's on. It just isn't showing anything. Looks like a loading screen that gave up.
Snow on every channel. The oldest weather in the world. Pixel says it used to be the late-night programme.
When the programmes were over? TV just … ended?
Grandpa's wardrobe. Three cardigans, all brown, all with tools in the pockets.
Right at the back there's a fourth cardigan. Green. He only wears it on special occasions. He hasn't found one yet.
A wire coat hanger. Empty and sad.
If I bend this here and twist that there … Looks like a bunny with reception. Promising.
There. Antenna. I'm officially a technician now.
A calendar. One day is circled in thick red. Either a birthday or the dentist.
And next to it, very small: "Ch3 – Waffleton".
Channel 3.
Channel 4. Looks like channel 3, only more boring.
A note. Grandpa, that's like a spoiler you're not allowed to read.
I hold it up to the light. All I see is Grandpa's thumbprint. I'd have recognised that anyway.
Did I just agree to this? I don't think I agreed to this –
Grandpa's first attempt at an underwater time machine. The fish didn't make it.
It has a snorkel. The fish. Grandpa really thought of everything. Except air.
A pyramid and a neon city. Grandpa has very broad taste. Or travel plans.
Grandpa drew crosses in the corner of the poster. Like destinations. Or shopping stops.
A toaster with a propeller. Flying breakfast. Never again.
There's still a crumb stuck to the propeller. It flew. I don't know how far. I don't want to know.
"Hits for Inventors, Volume 3". So there are two worse ones.
Grandpa ticked a song on the sleeve: "My Heart Is a Soldering Iron." I'm scared of the melody.

I'm not replugging myself. That's like soldering your own battery.
Pizza boxes. A stack up to the ceiling. The resistance lives on pizza and noodles. I could be happy here.
A towel on a hook. At least somebody here knows where their towel is.
The towel says "Don't Panic". Embroidered. The most reassuring thing in the whole base.
An old mainframe with tape reels. It's humming a nursery rhyme. That's either sweet or very worrying.
It's humming the nursery rhyme slower and slower. If it says it's afraid, I won't pull the plug. Promise.
The wreck's control desk. A hundred switches, no screen. Flying used to be handicraft.
One switch is labelled "Please don't". Another says "Really don't". The pilots were careful people.
A table with a mug at the edge. Black coffee so thick it holds the spoon in place. The mug is right at the edge. Right at it.
The mug wobbles when someone walks past. It stands there like a promise to fall off any second.
An old cleaning robot with a hat, in the corner, brown with rust. He looks like he used to have opinions.
There's a dent in his hat. And rust on his wheels. He's waiting for something. Maybe for someone with oil.
I give him a nudge. He tips over. I stand him back up. We're even.
An advertising poster. A food mixer in a flowery apron. "I know what's good for you." A world-domination AI that needs praise. This is going to be embarrassing. For her.
The food mixer on the poster is smiling. Food mixers shouldn't smile. That's a rule.
Two rebels. Leather jackets, sunglasses, noodles. It's night, it's indoors, and they still can't see a thing. On principle.
One of them has had a noodle in the corner of his mouth for minutes. Cool has its price.
Dog biscuits. Bone-shaped. Over there they were biscuits. I saw the transformation and I still don't believe it.
Dog biscuits. Still. I was hoping they'd be biscuits again the second time I looked.
A green code key. Over there. Here, a white plastic card from Mr Four. Both open the same thing. Only one of them fits in a trouser pocket.
Mr Four wanted to keep the card because of its corners. I counted them. There are four. He was right.
A fortune cookie. Over there a recipe card in joined-up writing. Here a cookie with a slip of paper. Logical. Sort of.
And where's Morphaeus now?
Which three rules?
Hey.
Hiss. A glass lid lifts. Max blinks into blue light. A wet cat is sitting on his chest.
Max pulls out the bag. Inside: bone-shaped dog biscuits.
You slept. I kept watch. That is the wrong distribution, and I'd like it on record.
I have been commenting. That's different.
Those are dog biscuits.
In your pocket.
Near me.
I've ended friendships for less.
Then go back. Now. And turn that thing back into something I can ignore.
I am everywhere now. Like background music. Only with content.
Your body is lying there smiling. I sit on the lid and keep watch. That's work. It isn't paid.
He lies there, smiling and drooling slightly. I've taken a photo. In my head. Forever.
Shake. With both paws. He'll wake up and pretend he woke up on his own.
Window open. Snow falls on the pod. Somewhere over there it's snowing now where it shouldn't. I am the weather.
Window shut. I'm wet. I'm always wet. That's the motto of this world.
The shaft is calling me. I can hear it. It says: crawl. I say: later. I'm a professional.
A shaft. Narrow, dark, metal. Any cat would go in there. I'm not any cat. I'm going anyway.
The shaft leads to the cooling system. Pipes, valves, a bucket of water. Someone tried cleaning here and gave up.
I tip the bucket over the cooling. Now it's raining over there. Indoors. I find that fair.
Paw on the switch. Click. Over there it's night. Here it gets … no brighter either. Click. Back on. I am the sun.
All empty. I checked. I checked every single one. It was a long afternoon.
Mine. From now on. It's dry, and I'm not. It's very simple maths.
A mug. At the edge. I can feel my ancestors watching me.
She underlined "good for you". Twice.
Don't you dare. I have dignity, fur and a memory.
A cookie with a note inside. It took humanity centuries to invent food that lies to you.
Cable round his neck, screwdriver in his mouth, headset. He smells of tea and panic. I sit on his laptop. He keeps typing. Respect.
She eats noodles in sunglasses, at night, indoors. I sit next to her and stare at the box. She gives me a noodle. One. Out of four.
Tool belt. I climb up it. He says nothing. The sunglasses say nothing either. We understand each other.
He beeps. I purr. We talk for a minute. He has opinions about Kalle that I won't repeat. But they're correct.
Rust. Expectation of coffee. A hat that smells of decades. There's someone grumpy in there. I like him already.
The pod smells of you. Of hoodie, rain and the rest of the soup. I lie down on the lid. Warm. Good. Take your time over there.
Keyboard. Warm. Exactly as wide as me. It was built for me, and someone forgot to tell me.
Pizza box, empty. The smell is still there. The smell is the cruellest thing about an empty box.
Towel. Dry. Cotton. I wrap myself up. I'm not coming out again. Call me when there's tuna.
He hums. I purr. We harmonise. Then he hums louder. He doesn't want to share. I understand.
Cold coffee. Thick. Smells like a week. I sniff it and I'm awake for three days.
Metal, draught, darkness. The shaft smells of adventure. I hate adventure. I'm going in anyway, because it's narrow.
A hundred switches. All smell of old fingers. None of fish. This ship never flew anywhere that had fish.
The poster smells of printer's ink and little flowers. I scratch the apron. She deserved it. As a precaution.
Bone-shaped. For dogs. I sniff once. I will never be able to make up for that one time.
A cookie with a note. I lick the cookie. The note tastes better. That says everything about fortune cookies.
The cell is cold and smells of metal. It's exactly as long as a … No. I'm not saying it. Not yet.
Kalle's typing. The rebels are eating. The mainframe is humming. And you're standing there like a loading bar.
Your pod is free. You could lie down. I'm not saying it as a reproach. I'm saying it as an expert.
You held your back while walking. Twice. I'm counting. Like Deckert counts the rain.
I like this resistance. It sleeps a lot.
Rusting. That's what you call it when someone stops tidying up. I know it from Max.
Noodles? From Mr Four. There are four.
The cat explained to us how to sleep properly. For forty minutes. We listened. We had no choice.
We are the resistance. We resist. For example, the urge to take off our sunglasses.
Greetings, lad. Please don't step on the floor, it's freshly mopped. Everything here is fresh. I've been mopping for nineteen years.
Nobody gets through there, lad. Except with a card. And except Sahra Konner. I'm looking for her. Have you seen her?
I don't know. It's on my job sheet. "Find Sahra Konner." Underneath: "Mop floor." I've done the second item.
My model series. They built a great many of us. All the same. None of us special. I'm the one with the mop. That is: all of us.
Not without a card, lad. With a card, gladly. I'll even hold the door. I hold all doors. That's the third item on my sheet.
My joints. Nineteen years of mopping. No oil. The oil can in my breast pocket has been empty for as long as I can think. I've been thinking for nineteen years.
Cheerio, lad. I'll be back. That is: I'm staying here. But it sounds better that way.
I'm a caretaker. I'm only looking for dirt.
Forty-seven. Forty-seven Sahra Konners. Lad, this is the happiest day of my working life.
I'll visit them all. One after another. Politely. I'll ring, I'll ask, I'll mop the entrance. Every one of them gets a clean entrance.
Cheerio, all. I'll be back. This time it's true.
… Lad. This is … I can't hear anything. I can't hear any squeaking. For the first time in nineteen years I can't hear myself.
You are my friend. That's a new item on the sheet. I'll write it right at the top. If you need me, lad: I'll come.
Lad, even with a card: Sahra Konner first. The sheet is clear. The sheet is my life.
A cookie with a note. Does it say Sahra Konner? No? Then I'll wipe up the crumbs before they fall.
One, mop. Two, find Sahra Konner. Three, hold doors. I've been on item two for nineteen years.
They all say that, lad. Then they leave again.
Here! Brought the drum. A line from here to your pod. Eighty metres of cable, two knots, one hope.
Done. On the way I'll tap into the AI's speaker, then you'll hear the cat in there too. I'm not doing you a favour. I know.
Hi. I need to get through there.
Who is Sahra Konner?
What does 08/15 mean?
Can you let me in?
Why do you squeak?
I'll be off then.
This is not the boy you're looking for.
Here. Sahra Konner. Forty-seven of them, with addresses.
Your joints. Here. Olive oil. From a world where people thought sport was a good idea.
No oil? Then he just keeps saying hello and squeaking. I feel sorry for him. A bit. As much as you can feel sorry for a robot.
He squeaks with every wipe. Sounds like a door asking for help.
A round armoured door in the concrete. Looks like the entrance to a vault where someone keeps their favourite recipe.
I knock. It sounds like knocking on a mountain. The mountain doesn't open.
Shut. Of course. I knock. The knock echoes. It echoes inside me because it doesn't arrive anywhere else.
A card reader with a little red light. Red means here what it means everywhere: no, but friendly.
The light glows red and a little sad. It hasn't let anyone in for a long time.
I hold up my hand with the stamp. "Human, provisional." The reader thinks. Red. It wanted a card, not a biography.
Card in. Green. The door rolls aside like a very slow curtain.
Behind it: no lab. A wall of glowing sockets and a thick cable. The lab isn't here. The lab is "on the line".
The sockets glow in rhythm. The lab is breathing. Through cables. I have to get in there. So, into the cables.
Now back to the pod, lie down, wake up in the lab. My CV is getting weirder and weirder.
A mop bucket. The water is cleaner than anything I've drunk today.
I'm not taking the bucket. The robot would notice. And he'd notice politely, which is the worst part.
A noticeboard with test results. Hundreds of slips. All with marks. All with a cake column. The cake column is empty.
Test subject 12: "Asked about the cake. Was reset." Test subject 33: "Did not ask about the cake. Was reset." Fair.
Yellow and black stripes on the floor. They say: caution. They don't say about what. That's design.
I stand on a yellow stripe. Nothing happens. I stand on a black one. Nothing either. Disappointing.
A lamp on the ceiling, dripping next to it. Someone mopped here for years, and it's still dripping. That's called Sisyphus with a mop.
The drop lands right next to the bucket. Every time. It's doing it on purpose.
A passage under the city. Neon behind me, concrete ahead. The city has a basement, and the basement has a door.
Something is humming somewhere at the back. Big and patient. Like a fridge that rules the world.
The robot's gone. The floor is still wet. He meant it to the very end.
On the floor is the last circle he mopped. A perfect circle. His farewell letter.
He mops in circles. Always circles. If he ever mops a straight line, something's happened.
Tuna for a robot. He'd politely accept the tin and politely have no idea what to do with it.
Dog biscuits for a caretaker. He has no dog. He has a mop. The mop doesn't eat.
And what are items one and two?
Nineteen years without oil. Let me see what I've got in my bag.
A robot who spent nineteen years on the second item because the first was too hard. I see myself in him.
In German, 08/15 means: standard. Nothing special. Run of the mill. People used to say it about things that did exactly what you expected.
He wears it on his chest. That's either very sad or very honest.
You just waved your hand and lied to a robot. I saw it. I'll see it again. In my dreams. For a laugh.
He's happy. A robot who was given a list is happy. I have a list and I'm not. There's no tuna on it.
I said it when we packed: for anything that squeaks. Tin heads included. Nobody listens to me, and yet I'm always right. That's my cross to bear.
He has fed me into a world-domination AI. I will be its loudspeaker. I've been worse. I've been wet.
Water in a bucket. On the floor. Drinkable. The first civilised facility in this world.
Test subject 47: "Very good, but asked for too little cake."
He mops in circles. I walk in circles before I lie down. We understand each other without talking.
He mops in circles. You stand in a circle. Only one of you gets paid for it. Neither, I think.
The door is round. You're square. That won't work as long as you only look at it.
Tin, smell of oil, damp mop. He bows to me. I allow it. First time in this world that someone understands rank.
The bucket smells of soap. I drink anyway. Soap is clean. Clean is good. I feel sick.
The armoured door smells of steel and secrets. Behind it: cables. Cables smell warm. Let me in.
Slips of paper, drawing pins, fear. Hundreds of test subjects and no cake. I can smell the disappointment. It smells like paper.
Three humans, one cat, one robot with a list. A good day. A wet one, but good.
Lad! Forty-seven Sahra Konners, forty-seven clean entrances. None of them was the right one. But they all said thank you. I'm content.
If you need me: I'll come. I'll be back. This time it's really true.
The lights over there are going out! The pods are opening! Half the city is waking up and it's hungry. Mr Four is going to get rich.
The cell. Glowing in the simulation, here cold and heavy as a … thing. I nearly called it something familiar. I didn't.
It's humming very quietly. Eternal, says Grandpa. I hope it has an off switch. Eternal is a long time.
The phone box. It's ringing like an advert.
Hello? … "Milk! Now even fresher!" It's the commercial break. Grandpa was right. Everything used to be possible. Even this.
Hiss. The lid rises. Max is holding a cold, long cell. Pixel is sitting on the edge pretending he was asleep.
Out on the street the phone box rings. Louder than usual. With a jingle.
You've got it. I had the window. We both worked. One of us got wet doing it.
I have to admit something. Reluctantly. You didn't once ask me for the solution.
I'm impressed. I'll never say that again. It was a slip of the tongue.
For you. Sounds like milk.
Wet in, wet out. I won't miss this world. Except the towel. I'm taking the towel.
Thanks, kid. We're moving now. Into a house with windows. We're keeping the sunglasses.
The man in the hat doesn't want correct answers. He wants human ones. That's not the same. Ask me.
Look at the people on the street. The crying man, the one with the umbrella, the one with the music. None of them is doing anything sensible. That's exactly what you need.
Right-click the crying man, the woman with the umbrella and the musician. Then their silliness goes in your notebook. Then go to the hat.
You have the answers in your notebook. Now you just have to say them instead of thinking. Should be easy for you.
For every question, the sensible answer fails. Pick the one that sounds like someone off the street said it.
Tortoise: argue with it. Rain: play the synthesizer. Soup: cry into it. I'm only saying this once. I've now said it once.
The man in the cardigan wants a recognition dish, the cook knows one number. You have to translate. You're bad at it, but it's only one number.
Two times two. How much is that? Don't tell me. Tell the cook.
Order "number four". Not two times two. Four. He only understands Four. I only understand tuna. Everyone has their word.
The machine wants to see a symptom, not hear one. Something that repeats. I never repeat myself. But I could. For payment.
Switch to me. I'll walk past the machine. Then again. Exactly the same. Then you switch back and tell the machine what you saw.
Press Tab, walk across the pavement in front of the machine twice as me, back to you, use the machine, choose "déjà vu". Done. I want fish for this.
Two lozenges. One makes it comfortable, one makes it true. You know which one you'd take. Take the other.
The blue one leads to the sofa. You've been there. For sixteen years.
Take the red one. I won't catch you. The man in the cardigan does that.
Granny knows you'll break the vase. She says it to your face. Use that. Anything said to your face can be turned around.
If something's going to happen anyway, you might as well get it over with. Tell her that. Politely. Granny-politely.
Ask her about the vase first, then say: "If I'm going to break it anyway, give it to me now." She'll sigh and hand it over. She already knows.
The door is shut and says nothing. The man in front is open and says everything. That's the wrong way round. Almost as if you could turn it round.
Squint and look at the door. Twice. There are words on it. Words can be moved.
Open code view, click "locked" on the door, click "talkative" on Schmidt. The door talks, he goes quiet, you walk through.
Only the original can send the copies away. They all wear slippers. But only one wears the word "original". You see words in code view.
You can't command the original. But you can command something you're holding. A cup, for example. Cups are copies. All of them.
Take the cup from the water cooler. Code view: swap "original" on the Schmidt at the very back with "copy" on the cup. Then the cup is in charge of everyone.
The cup is the boss now. Bosses give orders. Cups don't. So you have to do it for it.
What do you do with thirty employees who are in the way? You send them to lunch. I'd go along.
Use the cup on the clones and send them on lunch break. The original then gives you the sunglasses and the file. Voluntarily. Almost.
The tower has no exit. Your body does. It's lying here. Someone has to replug it. That someone has fur and can't see colours.
There are three colours with three shapes on the wall. Copy them down. Then type them at the terminal. I'll read along. Kalle will read it out. It'll be embarrassing.
Right-click the stripes, take the colour code, then use the terminal with the colour code. After that you switch to me.
Three cables, three sockets, one cat. The colours are no use to me, the shapes are. Circle, triangle, square are on both.
Circle to red, triangle to green, square to yellow. In the order on the wall. If Max quacks, it was the wrong one.
As me: cable with the circle into the red socket, triangle into green, square into yellow. Then he wakes up and acts as if it was his idea.
The tin head is looking for a woman. For nineteen years. He only has her name. Names are written down somewhere. On paper. In boxes.
There's a phone book in the phone box. She's in it. Forty-seven times. A caretaker with a list is a happy caretaker.
Rip the page "Konner, Sahra" out of the phone book and give it to the robot. He'll set off. If you have oil, oil him first. Then he'll like you. Someone has to.
There's no lab behind the armoured door, only a connection. The lab is a dream. You get there by cable. Kalle has cables. Kalle is cables.
The door needs a card. Mr Four has one. He'll trade it for his fourth ingredient. You have that. As a cookie. Don't be weird about it.
Card on the reader, use the port, Kalle lays the line. Then back to the pod and lie down. You'll wake up in the lab.
The switch wants weight. You have none. The cube has some. It just won't stand on it. It has a job description.
Code view. The cube says "heavy", you say "light". You know what words do when you click two of them.
Swap "heavy" from Bernd with "light" from you, then stand on the switch. Bernd will sulk afterwards. Get used to it. I have, for years.
The laser is deadly. The chicken is harmless. Two words hanging in the wrong place.
Take the chicken with you first. Then swap. A deadly chicken in your bag is still better than a deadly laser in your face.
Take the chicken off the plinth, code view: "deadly" from the laser for "harmless" from the chicken. Walk through the laser. It squeaks. That's it.
Two problems: a door that's shut and a cube standing in front of it. Two swaps. That's no coincidence. That's a curriculum.
The door was "locked" once before, and someone was "talkative". You know that swap. And for the cube you have something light in your bag. It squeaks.
First "locked" (door) for "talkative" (speaker). Then "heavy" (Bernd) for "light" (chicken). Bernd floats off, the door talks, you leave.
She sticks to three rules. You have three rules in your notebook. Hold them up to her. But not just any old way. Each answer tells you which one fits next.
Start with protecting. She'll say she protects you. Then ask about what she promised the protected. Then say why it never existed.
Rule 1, then rule 2, then rule 3. Protecting, cake, sugar. She'll think for a moment and then not at all for a very long time.
The cell is hot. You have something cold with you. Or you know someone who can open a window. Either works. One of them is me.
Code view: the cell says "hot", the biscuits in your bag say "cold". Or: switch to me, I'll open the window above your pod. Snow.
Swap "hot" from the cell with "cold" from the biscuits. Or: Tab, use the ceiling window in the base as me. Then take the cell. Then home.
Mr Four has been looking for an ingredient for eleven years. Granny gave it to you. In joined-up writing. Out here it looks different. Everything looks different out here.
Look in your inventory. The recipe card has turned into a cookie. With a note. Who reads notes from cookies? Cooks, apparently.
Give Mr Four the fortune cookie. He'll break it open, cry, cook and give you the card for the armoured door. All in four minutes.
Kalle can't translate anything because he lost his table. The rusty bucket in the corner has a copy. He just needs a reason to wake up.
See the mug at the edge of the table? See the bucket under it? See me? I'm a cat. I think you can see where this is going.
Switch to me and use Kalle's mug. It falls. The coffee wakes Piepsi. Piepsi prints the table. I take no responsibility. I never do.
Still calculating. Please wait. I only say that because every toaster here says it.
A page from the phone book. Sahra Konner, forty-seven times. One of them is bound to pick up.
I've never ripped a page out of a book before. I feel like a rebel. A very small one, with a paper cut.
Red. The truth, says Morphaeus. Probably tastes of strawberry and consequences.
I'm holding the truth in my hand. It's small, round and a bit sticky. I'd imagined it bigger.
Blue. Wake up, forget everything, sofa. Honestly, that doesn't sound too bad.
I'm keeping it. Not to swallow. As a reminder that once I made the uncomfortable choice.
Grandma's biscuits in the bag. Cold, but they still smell of Sunday. I'm not allowed to eat one. I just know.
The biscuits are oven-warm. The cell gave off its heat, and the biscuits took it. Best oven in the world.
Steam is rising from my bag. I smell like a bakery on the run.
Schmidt's sunglasses. I put them on for a second. Everything gets darker and I look more important. I take them off before anyone sees.
With these on I could lean back and dodge bullets. Without them I only dodge homework.
Schmidt's file. A glowing data file that hums when I hold it. Rule 1 is in it. And a report about me.
I'm not reading the report about me again. "Suspiciously human." That's enough for a lifetime.
Circle red, triangle green, square yellow. My handwriting. Looks like a recipe for very colourful maths.
I'm learning it by heart. Circle red, triangle green, square yellow. Sounds like a nursery rhyme nobody wants to sing.
A green code key. It glows in my bag like a phone with a new message. For me. At last.
The key is made of numbers running downwards. If you look long enough, you see blonde, brunette, redhead. So they say. I just see numbers.
The portal device. Without a battery it's just a very expensive thing that points at walls. Grandpa's living room was so close.
Please insert AA battery. Don't have one. I've got a rubber chicken and problems. The universe always gives me the wrong thing.
A rubber chicken. If I squeeze it, it squeaks. If I don't, it looks reproachful.
The energy cell. Frosty and harmless now. I'm carrying the final boss in my trouser pocket, and it's as cold as an ice lolly.
It's misting up my pocket from the inside. I now have air-conditioned trousers.
The cell is glowing in my pocket. I can feel it through three layers of fabric. Grandpa, you owe me a pair of trousers.
The bag rustles every time you move. I can hear it. I hear everything that rustles. It's a gift and a torment.
A chicken with a hole in the middle. People used to hang those on ropes and ride across chasms. Don't ask any more.
You smell like an iron. I'm sitting on you anyway. Warmth is warmth.
She sounds like the school secretary, only with lasers.
A device on the wall. White, with a handle and an orange tip. It looks like I'm not allowed to touch it. So I'm touching it.
The handle says "Property of the lab". And underneath, scribbled: "Good luck".
I pull it out of the mount. It hums. It has a trigger. I've played too many games not to know what comes next.
… That was Grandpa. In the living room. For one second. And the first thing he asks about is milk.
The device is dead. One second of portal, then a battery warning. Like my phone, only with a living room.
Hi, Bernd.
A big red button in the floor. It wants weight. I'm the opposite of weight. I'm sofa average.
I stand on it. Jump. Nothing. The button has higher standards than I do.
I stand on it. Nothing. It doesn't even notice me. That's the second time today a floor has ignored me.
Bernd. Grey cube, googly eyes, smiley. He floats. In code view it says "heavy". A floating cube is heavy. Sure.
There's a heart on his side. I'm probably not supposed to love him. Too late.
I push him to the switch. He floats back. I push him again. He floats back. Bernd has principles.
A cake in the corner. Made of cardboard. With a painted candle. At least it's honest.
I tap it. It falls over. On the back it says: "Cake (symbolic)".
An exit door. Shut. It opens when the switch is pressed. I know because M.U.T.T.I. said so three times.
The door says "Exit". It means it. Just not right now.
A round loudspeaker in the ceiling. An AI and a cat come out of it. Neither lets the other finish.
The speaker crackles before anyone talks. I flinch every time. It knows that.
White panels. Square. A hundred of them. All the same. Whoever works here dreams in tiles.
One panel has a fingerprint. One. Someone was here before me. And was alive.
An empty mount. The portal device hung there. Now only my disappointment hangs there.
I put my hand in the mount. It fits. Doesn't help.
I'm "light". It says so. On me. In green. That's the first compliment in this world, and it comes from a label.
Oh. I'm … heavy. Every step feels like Monday. But the switch is waiting.
Bernd. Bernd, I didn't mean it like that. I just needed your weight. … That sounded wrong.
And the cake?
Of course it is.
The cardboard cake is heavy now. It's standing in the corner weighing a ton. The switch is not in the corner.
Bernd is honest now. He says nothing, but he means it. The cardboard cake is heavy and doesn't float. Nothing gained.
The switch is "tired" now. It won't even press itself any more. I'm "unpressed". I was that before too.
Portal device on the cake. Nothing. Not even a beep. Two dummies looking at each other.
Tuna for Bernd. He has no mouth. He has a sticker. The sticker smiles anyway.
Wooden spoon on the portal device. Portal too small. Spoon too big. And the battery's dead anyway.
Hello, test subject. Welcome to the programme for your own good. I am M.U.T.T.I. I know what's good for you. It says so on my poster too.
There is a cat in my loudspeaker. That is rude. I am ignoring it. For your own good.
After every test there is cake. That is rule 2. I keep to rules. You will learn to appreciate that.
The device was a gift. The battery was not. One has to set priorities. For your own good.
Chamber one. The floor switch opens the door. It needs weight. You don't bring any. That wasn't meant personally. Yes it was.
This is your companion cube. His name is Bernd. He will never leave you. Unless you leave him. Then it's your fault.
The cube does not stand on switches. It accompanies. Read the job description.
Very good. Test passed. You won't manage this, but I believe in you. That was for the next chamber. I like to be prepared.
Your cake is in another test chamber.
Resetting. As with all my test subjects.
No swaps left. You may leave and come back. I forget nothing. But I pretend to. For your own good.
White. White everywhere. Max is standing in a chamber of panels that all look the same. A red button in the floor. A door. A loudspeaker.
Max pulls the trigger. A shimmering round hole opens in the wall. Behind it: Grandpa's living room. Grandpa on the sofa, cup of tea in his hand.
Swap: heavy (Bernd) ↔ light (Max). Bernd slowly rises. Max's trainers press grooves into the floor.
Click. The door slides open. Bernd turns away and floats up to the ceiling in a huff.
Did you remember the milk?
I can hear that. I can hear everything. Kalle put me in the ceiling. I am now this chamber's conscience. A very tired conscience.
